title: Binary Search Trees
summary: The BST invariant and its search/insert/delete/validate/kth-element operations — the ordering property that turns a tree into a decision structure.

slides.markdown:
A **binary search tree** adds one invariant on top of an ordinary binary tree: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger. That single rule turns the tree into a decision structure — at every node, comparing your target against the node's value tells you which subtree the answer must live in, discarding the other subtree entirely.

That's what makes search, insert, and delete all O(height) instead of O(n): each step eliminates roughly half the remaining candidates, the same divide-and-conquer idea behind binary search on a sorted array, adapted to a structure that supports efficient insertion. The catch, covered later in this group, is that height isn't guaranteed to stay small — that's exactly the gap self-balancing trees close.

slides.subTitle: Following the invariant down to a null slot
slides.markdown:
Search: compare the target to the current node. Equal, you're done. Smaller, recurse left. Larger, recurse right. Hit a null pointer, the target isn't in the tree.

Insert follows the identical path-finding logic, but instead of stopping at null, it **creates** a new node there. Because the new node's position was found by respecting the invariant at every step down, the invariant is automatically preserved — the new node is smaller than everything on its path that went right, and larger than everything that went left, which is exactly what "belongs in this position" means.

slides.subTitle: Leaf, one child, two children
slides.markdown:
Deleting a node with **no children** is trivial — just remove it, replace the parent's pointer with null. Deleting a node with **exactly one child** is nearly as simple — splice the child up into the deleted node's position, since there's nothing to reconcile.

Deleting a node with **two children** is the genuinely hard case: you can't just remove it, because both its children need a new place in the tree, and neither can simply take the parent's old slot without breaking the BST invariant for the other. The standard fix — replace the deleted value with its inorder successor (or predecessor) — is covered in full on the next slide.

slides.subTitle: Via inorder successor (or predecessor) swap

slides.sectionTitle: Validating a BST by checking only the immediate parent

slides.subTitle: Using a (min, max) bound passed down the recursion
slides.markdown:
```python
def is_valid_bst(node, low=float('-inf'), high=float('inf')):
    if not node:
        return True
    if not (low < node.val < high):
        return False
    return (is_valid_bst(node.left, low, node.val) and
            is_valid_bst(node.right, node.val, high))
```

Each recursive call carries the full valid range inherited from **every** ancestor, not just the immediate parent — going left tightens the upper bound to the current node's value, going right tightens the lower bound. This correctly catches violations from any ancestor at any depth, not just the direct parent.

An equally valid alternative: run an inorder traversal and confirm the output is strictly increasing — since a BST's inorder traversal is sorted if and only if the tree is valid, this sidesteps bound-tracking entirely at the cost of building the full traversal output.

slides.subTitle: And the early-exit optimization
slides.markdown:
Since inorder traversal of a BST produces ascending order, the kth smallest element is simply the kth value that traversal produces — and crucially, you don't need to traverse the whole tree to get it: stop the moment you've counted k values, which is a genuine early exit, not just a stylistic choice, since continuing past that point does no useful work.

Kth largest is the mirror image: traverse in **reverse**-inorder order (right, node, left instead of left, node, right), which produces descending order, and again stop after k values. Both variants are O(h + k) rather than O(n) in the typical case, since you only ever descend as far as necessary to reach the kth value, not visit every node in the tree.

slides.subTitle: Without extra pointers
slides.markdown:
Four related "find the nearest value" queries, all solvable in O(h) using only the BST invariant, no parent pointers or extra structures needed:

- **Floor(x)** — the largest value ≤ x. Walk down; each time the current node's value ≤ x, record it as a candidate and go right (there might be something closer, larger, still ≤ x); each time it's > x, go left.
- **Ceiling(x)** — the mirror image: track the smallest value ≥ x, going left when a candidate is found, right otherwise.
- **Successor(x)** — if x has a right subtree, its successor is that subtree's leftmost node (smallest value greater than x). If not, the successor is the nearest ancestor for which x is in the left subtree — found by walking down from the root tracking the last node where you went left.
- **Predecessor(x)** — the exact mirror of successor, using the left subtree's rightmost node, or the nearest ancestor for which x is in the right subtree.

All four reuse the identical single-pass, invariant-guided walk — no new algorithmic idea beyond search itself.

slides.sectionTitle: BST vs sorted array vs hash map
slides.subTitle: When ordered operations justify the tree
slides.markdown:
| | Sorted array | Hash map | BST (balanced) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Search | O(log n) | O(1) average | O(log n) |
| Insert/delete | O(n) (shifting) | O(1) average | O(log n) |
| Range queries ("all values between x and y") | O(log n + k) | not supported | O(log n + k) |
| Ordered iteration | free (already sorted) | not supported | free (inorder) |

A hash map wins on raw search speed but gives up ordering entirely — no "next largest," no range queries, no sorted iteration. A sorted array keeps ordering but pays O(n) for any insert or delete. A balanced BST is the structure that keeps ordering **and** gets O(log n) insert/delete, which is exactly why it's the right choice whenever a problem needs both fast mutation and ordered queries — anything less than that, and a simpler structure usually wins on constants.

slides.sectionTitle: Sorted input degrading a BST's insert order
slides.subTitle: Into a linked list
slides.markdown:
Inserting values in already-sorted order into a plain BST (no rebalancing) produces the worst possible shape: every new value is larger (or smaller) than everything already inserted, so each one becomes the current rightmost (or leftmost) node's only child — a straight chain, structurally a linked list, with height O(n) instead of O(log n).

```python
# inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into an empty BST
# produces: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, each with only a right child
```

Every operation that should be O(log n) — search, insert, delete — silently degrades to O(n) on this shape, with no error or warning; the code is entirely correct, just pathologically slow on this specific input pattern. This is precisely the motivation for self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black), covered in the next-but-one topic, which guarantee O(log n) height regardless of insertion order.

slides.sectionTitle: The BST invariant as a recurring theme
slides.markdown:
Every operation in this topic — search, insert, delete, validate, kth-element, floor/ceiling — is really the same move applied to a different question: use the ordering invariant to eliminate half the remaining tree at each step, the way binary search eliminates half an array.

That single idea is worth internalizing precisely because so many BST interview problems are variations on it rather than new algorithms — recognizing "this is just search/insert/delete with a small twist" is usually faster and more reliable than deriving a new approach from scratch. The one thing this idea doesn't protect against is the tree's shape itself degrading under adversarial insertion order, which is exactly the gap the rest of this group's advanced tree topics close.
